newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria celebrates after Socialists quit.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria celebrates after Socialists quit.

text.p: Despite looming hardship hundreds of dancing and singing Bulgarians poured in to the streets of central Sofia to celebrate the ruling Socialists' decision to step down from power two years ahead of scheduled elections.
Bulgaria's ex-communist ruling party caved in to opposition pressure on Tuesday after 30 days of mass protests, agreeing to general elections by April 20.

"There is still a great deal of uncertainty. The fuel shortages, the bread queues, the astronomic prices and meagre wages will be around for some time, but there is hope," Petar Bonev, a software expert told Reuters.

Hundreds of students and teen-agers danced to the tunes of a popular rock group in front of the gold-domed Alexander Nevski Cathedral, the site of daily oppostion rallies for the past month. They chanted "We won".
"I am happy that bloodshed was avoided, I feared a violent crack down," said Anna Petrova, a middle-aged accountant.
Hundreds of cars flying the national flags honked their horns and protesters dismantled roadblocks which had recently sprung up around the city.
City buses and trams, which were on strike for two days resumed work. Students danced around blazing tyres in front of the University building, where they had a major roadblock a few hours ago.
"Now Bulgaria has more chances of becoming part of Europe, where it belongs, rather then being led against its will into the third world," said Dimitar Karaangelov, a school teacher.
The Socialists and the opposition parties agreed on Tuesday to early elections after meeting President Petar Stoyanov.

"I do not promise you that you will be richer or you will live better, I promise you that under the next government I will be honest and you will be master of your lives," Stoyanov told jubilant supporters as they lifted him onto their shoulders and carried him through the streets.
Stoyanov said Bulgaria was faced with severe challenges.
Inflation was more than 50 percent in January, the biggest oil refinery is running out of crude because it cannot pay its bills, and people queued for bread in the capital on Tuesday.
The political crisis accelerated the collapse of the lev, which closed at 2,800-3,000 levs to the dollar on Tuesday from 1,000 a week ago.
Sky-rocketing prices on goods have shrunk demand to basic goods and many shops have closed down.

"I do not mind the hard times through which we will have to pass as long as I know that after this period of hardship Bulgaria will be a country where my children and I will have a future," Iliana Petrova, a philosophy student, told Reuters.
The Socialists, elected to a four-year term in 1994, have been blamed for the crisis.
Outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned on December 21 but the party had insisted on forming a new cabinet until Tuesday when it yielded to popular pressure.
The International Monetary Fund welcomed the resolution of the deadlock and voiced hopes for resumption of loan talks with the cash-strapped country. REUTER
